title: Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0010】Prompt and accurate disease diagnosis represents a cornerstone in optimizing treatment outcomes, typically achieved via the detection of pathognomonic biomarkers [1] (Fig. 1A). Ideal diagnostic modalities demand rapid turnaround, high sensitivity, and robust fidelity. Conventional analytical techniques include polymerase chain reaction (PCR) [2], lateral-flow immunometric assays [3], electrochemical methods [4], DNA sequencing, microfluidics [5,6] and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) [7]. Despite their utility, these classical frameworks routinely require high-precision instrumentation, cost-prohibitive reagents, intricate sample preparation steps, and time-consuming quantification protocols [8]. Moreover, they remain fundamentally limited in terms of real-time monitoring capabilities and in vivo sensitivity. Genetically encoded biosensors offer a compelling alternative by capturing target biomolecular inputs and transducing them into quantifiable output signals, thereby emerging as a promising strategy for biomarker detection. The distinct advantages of these biosensors lie in their capacity for rapid, sensitive, non-invasive, cost-effective, and real-time monitoring [9,10].Typically, a genetically encoded biosensor comprises three interconnected functional modules: a sensing module that detects specific inputs (e.g., metabolites, chemical cues, or environmental stimuli), a regulatory module tasked with signal transduction, and an output module that generates a reporter signal [11].

【Introduction · p0015】Genetically encoded biosensors primarily operate via mechanisms such as allosteric transcription factors (aTFs), two-component systems (TCSs), Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET), and nucleic acid-based architectures. FRET- and nucleic acid-based systems have been widely deployed in diagnostics due to their high sensitivity, operational efficiency, and real-time, second-scale monitoring capabilities without latency, which has been comprehensively reviewed elsewhere [[12], [13], [14], [15], [16]]. Nevertheless, transcriptional regulation-based frameworks (specifically aTFs and TCSs) hold unparalleled promise for next-generation intelligent theranostics. Crucially, transcriptional regulation-based biosensors not only possess exceptional signal amplification and high modularity, but also directly couple biomarker detection to sustained functional outputs. This enables their seamless integration into closed-loop “monitoring-treatment” circuits, where biomarker detection drives the autonomous activation of therapeutic modules for disease intervention. While transcriptional circuits inherently encounter limitations including kinetic latency, basal leakage, and host metabolic burden, advanced engineering strategies are steadily mitigating these drawbacks, reinforcing their role as a cornerstone of intelligent genetic circuits. Due to this distinctive advantage of aTF- and TCS-based biosensors, this review focuses on the current development and emerging potential of these two classes of biosensors for the detection of disease relevant biomarkers. Characteristically, an aTF modulates target gene expression by governing the binding of RNA polymerase to DNA, structurally mediated by a DNA-binding domain (DBD) and an effector-binding domain (BD). Conversely, a classical TCS consists of a membrane-bound histidine kinase (HK), featuring an extracytoplasmic N-terminal stimulus-sensing domain and a cytosolic C-terminal autokinase domain, and a cytosolic response regulator (RR). Upon activation, the HK catalyzes its own autophosphorylation and sequentially transfers the phosphoryl group to the RR, which subsequently regulates gene expression (Fig. 1B). The performance of these genetically encoded biosensors can be quantitatively benchmarked via dose-response profiles (Fig. 1C). To satisfy diverse clinical requirements, key biophysical parameters—including reporter expression intensity, substrate binding affinity, and DNA binding affinity—can be rationally tuned to tailor operational sensitivity and specificity [17].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【From quantitative description to system-level design · p0235】Genetically encoded biosensors function as core interfaces that translate molecular inputs into programmable cellular outputs, thereby enabling the integration of environmental sensing with synthetic gene circuits and downstream therapeutic responses. From a systems perspective, their performance is not solely determined by individual components but emerges from the coordinated operation of the entire input–sensing–processing–output cascade. Accordingly, optimizing biosensor function requires a unified framework that links quantitative system behavior to multi-layer circuit design.

【From quantitative description to system-level design · p0240】The functional behavior of genetically encoded biosensors is quantitatively described by their dose–response relationship, which captures how variations in input signal concentration are transformed into output signal intensity. This relationship provides a generalizable basis for both evaluating and engineering biosensor performance. Several key parameters are widely used to characterize this response. Basal leakage represents the background output in the absence of input, reflecting intrinsic system noise. Dynamic range describes the maximal change in output relative to this baseline (i.e., fold induction), indicating signal amplitude. The response threshold (θ), often defined as the half-maximal effective concentration (EC50), determines the operational concentration window of the sensor. Response sensitivity, = ’ corresponding to the slope of the dose–response curve near the threshold, reflects how sharply the system responds to changes in input signal [212,213]. Together, these parameters define a multidimensional performance landscape in which biosensor behavior can be quantitatively interpreted.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion and perspectives · p0375】Looking forward, addressing the inherent limitations of transcriptional biosensors relative to post-transcriptional and post-translational sensors is a key frontier in synthetic biology. As highlighted in this article, while transcriptional sensors (aTFs and TCSs) excel at executing complex logic operations and driving high-level expression of therapeutic actuators, their response dynamics are fundamentally constrained by the multi-step processes of transcription and translation. In contrast, protein- or RNA-based sensors offer near-instantaneous signal transduction, but often at the expense of lower signal gain or limited actuation capacity. To bridge these performance gaps, the lineage of next generation intelligent biological systems will transcend traditional transcription factor paradigms by incorporating rapidly evolving molecular tools. Specifically, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) based biosensors offer unprecedented nucleic acid recognition capabilities with single nucleotide specificity, while programmable RNA regulators, such as toehold switches and riboswitches, enable versatile post transcriptional control with minimal genetic footprints. To bypass the historical liabilities of cell toxicity, low transfection efficiency, and stringent biological containment, cell free synthetic biology has emerged as a high-fidelity deployment platform. Operating outside living boundaries, cell free platforms preserve complex enzymatic networks within paper based or polymeric matrices, providing robust, shelf stable point of care diagnostics that bridge the gap between abstract synthetic networks and pragmatic clinical deployment.

【Conclusion and perspectives · p0385】Beyond data analysis, computational approaches are expected to play an increasingly important role in biosensor design and optimization. Integration of multi-omics datasets may accelerate the identification of clinically relevant biomarkers and guide the engineering of sensing modules with improved specificity, sensitivity, and tunability. The historical reliance on trial-and-error screening is increasingly replaced by artificial intelligence assisted circuit design, where deep learning algorithms predict protein conformation, optimize promoter strength, and mitigate genetic cross talk before experimental execution. In parallel, advances in protein design, regulatory circuit engineering, and host chassis development will further expand the functional scope of biosensors, enabling detection of increasingly complex physiological states (Fig. 4).

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · fig1】Fig. 1 Overview of genetically encoded biosensors for disease biomarker detection and clinical application. (A) Representative diseases and their corresponding biomarkers across various human systems. (B) Core architecture of a genetically encoded biosensor, consisting of sensing, regulating, and output modules. (C) Optimization of biosensor performance parameters such as sensitivity, dynamic range, threshold, and basal leakage, with the goal of tailoring the sensor response curve to meet precise clinical needs. (D) Translational applications from laboratory prototypes to clinical utility, including portable diagnostics, wearable devices, and living microbial platforms."

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Engineered biosensors for biomarker diagnosis and theranostic circuits. (A) CpxAR-based glucose diagnostic system. Glucose triggers CpxA kinase activity and subsequent CpxR phosphorylation ("P"), driving target gene transcription. Solid arrows denote protein expression; dashed arrows indicate CpxAR signal transduction and allostery. Hydrogel encapsulation enables glucose quantification in clinical samples. (B) Phenylalanine-responsive theranostic circuit. Phenylalanine-induced dimerization of a human PAH-derived module activates phenylalanine-degrading enzymes. Alginate-encapsulated cells effectively reduce toxic metabolites in human blood and mouse models. (C) A diagnostic system for bile acids with environmental adaptability. Utilizing the VFA0359 regulator and genetic logic gates, engineered bacteria specifically activate in the mammalian gut while remaining dormant in external environments. (D) A theranostic circuit utilizing the HucR repressor. Uric acid binding induces dissociation of the KRAB-HucR fusion protein, triggering signal output and uricase production, which maintains healthy serum uric acid levels and reduces renal crystal deposition in mouse models.

【Fig. 3 · fig3】Fig. 3 Comprehensive engineering strategies for optimizing the dose response landscape of genetically encoded biosensors as well as computational and machine learning approaches for sensor engineering, regulatory-element optimization, circuit design, and DBTL-guided iteration. The central diagram illustrates the interconnected performance parameters including sensitivity, dynamic range, response threshold, basal leakage, and stability. (A) Dynamic range amplification techniques involve increasing gene dosage, changing promoter and ribosome binding sites, or deploying multistage transcriptional cascades to maximize signal output. (B) Basal leakage reduction strategies minimize background noise by strengthening DNA binding affinities through directed mutations, optimizing core promoter sequences, or implementing posttranscriptional suppression via antisense RNA and degradation tags. (C) Response threshold modulation adjusts the operational sensing window by altering the ligand binding affinity of the regulatory module or by modifying the intracellular expression levels of the relevant transcription factors and two component systems. (D) Sensitivity enhancement focuses on steepening the response curve by increasing intracellular ligand concentrations through membrane transporter engineering, or by improving allosteric and phosphortransfer efficiencies. (E) System stability reinforcement ensures reliable long-term performance in complex environments through the chromosomal integration of genetic elements and the implementation of robust stabilizer circuits to buffer against external perturbations.
